headline: White House asks Congress to save full-spectrum CBD by 11 December
dek: A White House funding-issues list asks Congress to rewrite the hemp definition so nonintoxicating full-spectrum CBD survives the 11 December THC cap.
key_points: A White House document on FY 2027 continuing-resolution issues lists a USDA 'Hemp Definition' change as a priority that needs new statutory authority.
It asks Congress to update the definition of final hemp-derived cannabinoid products so nonintoxicating full-spectrum CBD stays available, with guardrails to keep products from children.
The request sets no THC limit and does not seek to save intoxicating hemp products such as THC drinks, according to The Marijuana Herald.
The federal cap of 0.4 mg of total THC per container and current government funding both run out on the same day: 11 December 2026.
body: The White House has asked Congress to change federal hemp law so that nonintoxicating full-spectrum CBD products stay on the market when the new federal THC limits take effect. The request appears in a document titled 'FY 2027 Continuing Resolution (CR) Appropriations Issues', which lists items the administration wants handled in the next government funding bill, according to The Marijuana Herald, which reported it on 23 November.

In a section for the Agriculture Department headed 'Hemp Definition', the document marks the change as a legislative priority that requires additional statutory authority. It asks for language updating the definition of final hemp-derived cannabinoid products to preserve access to nonintoxicating full-spectrum CBD, with guardrails to keep such products away from children, while keeping Congress's aim of restricting products that pose serious health risks. The document was first shared publicly by cannabis commentator Anthony Varrell on X; we have not seen it published on a government site.

The restriction comes from the law President Trump signed in November 2025, which redefined hemp around total THC and limits finished hemp products to 0.4 milligrams of THC per container. Full-spectrum CBD products are made from whole-plant extracts and keep the trace THC that occurs naturally in hemp. Many of them cannot meet a per-container cap that low, so they would fall outside the hemp definition along with the intoxicating products the law was aimed at.

As we reported on 12 November, the first phase of the law took effect that day, removing products made with cannabinoids the plant cannot produce naturally. Congress pushed most of the remaining limits, including the per-container cap, to 11 December. That is also the day current government funding expires, which is why the hemp fix is being negotiated as part of the spending package.
> The White House is trying to separate two products the 2025 law treated as one: the CBD tincture that never got anyone high, and the THC seltzer that did.
## What the request does and does not do

The request is narrow. According to the Herald, it names no THC number, so it does not say how much trace THC a full-spectrum product could carry. It also does not seek to preserve intoxicating hemp products, including THC beverages. Anyone hoping the administration would rescue the broader hemp THC trade will find nothing here.

The request also fits a pattern. The Herald notes that a December 2025 executive order directed White House officials to work with Congress on preserving full-spectrum CBD access, and that a June supplemental appropriations proposal formally asked for changes to the hemp definition. On 18 November, as we reported, a White House spokeswoman said only that the administration was still exploring hemp rules. The funding-issues list is the first concrete statement of what it wants from the December bill.
## The bills competing for the same slot

The White House is not the only voice. As we reported on 18 November, Senators Tim Sheehy and Amy Klobuchar have introduced a Hemp Guardrails Act that would replace the 11 December cliff with a regulatory framework built around a 1% total THC limit and a 21-and-over sales rule. Other lawmakers want the ban to start on time. The Herald says Congress could use the funding bill to revise the definition, delay the limits again, or carve out exemptions for particular products.

Each option has a different result for operators. A narrow CBD carve-out would protect wellness brands and the farmers who supply them, but leave THC drinks and edibles on course for removal. A delay would buy everyone time without settling the rules. A full framework such as the Sheehy-Klobuchar bill would keep a larger part of the market legal under new limits. Only a change to the statute can do any of this; agencies cannot waive the definition on their own, which is why the document says new authority is needed.

For CBD makers, the document is the strongest signal yet that their product category has a sponsor inside the administration. It is not law, and the wording Congress adopts, if any, will decide which products qualify. Firms selling full-spectrum products should expect any carve-out to come with conditions on labeling, packaging and sales to minors, since the request ties access to keeping products from children.

For retailers and distributors of intoxicating hemp products, nothing in this request changes the 11 December date. State regulators are already preparing: as we reported, Maine, Vermont, Iowa and Rhode Island have told sellers how they will apply the federal cap.

Watch the text of the continuing resolution as it is drafted in the next two weeks. The key questions are whether it carries any hemp language at all, whether that language is limited to full-spectrum CBD or extends further, and whether it sets a THC number. If Congress passes a funding bill with no hemp changes, the 0.4 mg per-container cap applies from 11 December.
